title: Kids Say the Darndest Things
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane, writing as a second-year math teacher, reflects on a student who froze while choosing a scale for a scatter plot. He had given students a rule for picking a scale, and this student had already applied it correctly when he began prompting her step by step. Her actual obstacle was a misconception he had not anticipated, namely how to plot a value of 900 on an axis whose scale starts at 1,000. Kane concludes that his reflex to simplify steps she already understood was a disservice that signaled low expectations. He then questions whether students might learn more by struggling with less direction, and admits he does not know how to facilitate that. It is a short, candid teacher reflection on diagnosing misconceptions and the limits of over-scaffolding.
points: Students who struggle most with math often hold misconceptions a teacher would never predict, such as being unsure where a value below the first scale mark goes.
Kane gave a procedural rule for choosing a scale reluctantly, since he would rather students reason it out intuitively.
Over-prompting steps a student has already completed can signal that the teacher doubts her ability.
He wonders whether less teacher direction and early failure would produce more ownership of understanding, and is honest that he lacks the craft to facilitate it.
quotes: But a number of students cannot find an appropriate scale, and freeze up when asked to try. So I reluctantly gave them a rule -- divide the maximum by the number of lines on the coordinate plane you want to use, and round up.

It took me a moment to realize that she had gone through all of the reasoning I was directing her through, and she had a misconception I hadn't even considered. Much of the data we work with is in the range of 1-20, and we don't see many values below the scale of the axes.

I was pretty humbled by my inability to predict student misconceptions from students who have the most trouble with math. As I have been throughout this year. That is the skill that, as a new teacher, I didn't have at the beginning of the year, and I'm still just developing.

My first reflex was to dumb down pieces of the question that my student had already comprehended -- doing her a disservice in the process, sending the message that I didn't think she could do what she had already done, and done faithfully given my instruction.

What if she would learn better by getting less direction from me, failing at first, but eventually owning her own understanding, in a way that she clearly didn't given what she showed in class today? I don't know. And I don't know how to facilitate that kind of understanding.
